description: Authored rationale for the HU single-raised-pot turn nodes (S6): the 2nd-barrel decision (hero = flop c-bettor) and facing a turn barrel (hero = flop caller). Keyed by hero/counterpart pairing; scoring itself lives in backend/app/domain/postflop.py (grade_turn_barrel / grade_vs_turn_bet). Source: docs/research/02-postflop-strategy.md §5.1-5.2, 5.4.

rationale_parts.lead: The big blind called your flop bet; whether to barrel (fire a second bet) depends on what the turn card did to their calling hands.
points: Overcards and board-pairing turns weaken the pairs they called with — keep firing.
Turns that complete a flush or straight IMPROVE the caller's range: check back more without a real hand or key blockers.
Blank turns are give-ups with pure air — they already showed they'll continue, so a bluff needs a scare card or new equity to stay believable.

rationale_parts.lead: From the cutoff the second barrel leans more toward value than the button's — your tighter flop c-bet range means your barrels should mean it.
points: Fire turns that pair the board or bring an overcard — they hit your Broadway-heavy range harder than the big blind's calls.
Keep barreling strong hands and big combo draws for value and protection.
With a medium pair on a blank, check back: a marginal hand cashes in by reaching showdown cheaply, not by betting into the hands that continue.

rationale_parts.lead: UTG's barrels are the most believable in the game on high cards — and the most punishable everywhere else.
points: An overcard or board-pairing turn almost always fits your narrow, strong story: keep betting.
But the big blind's flop call was made knowing your range is strong — on draw-completing turns and low blanks their wider range catches up fast.
Give up your weakest bluffs sooner than the later seats would.

rationale_parts.lead: A second barrel from the button is much stronger news than the flop c-bet — they bet flops with almost anything, but turn bets lean toward value and real draws.
points: Start from pot odds (the price the bet offers you): that decides how strong a hand you need, and a marginal pair that could call the flop often can't call a big turn bet.
On blank turns nothing changed — disciplined calls with decent pairs keep their value.
On scare turns (draws complete, overcards land) their story is believable: folding a marginal hand at a bad price is discipline, not a leak.

rationale_parts.lead: Facing a cutoff double barrel, work out the price before you think about your hand.
points: The cutoff's turn-betting range is tighter and more value-heavy than the button's, so marginal made hands continue less often — especially on turns that favor their Broadway-heavy range.
Strong hands and good draws continue: a draw wants the right price on one card to come.
Pure air has no business trying to catch bluffs out of position against a second barrel.

rationale_parts.lead: A UTG double barrel is the most value-heavy line you'll face from the blinds: at live stakes it's rarely a bluff.
points: Their flop c-bet from a narrow range already signalled strength — a turn bet on top of it means it.
Fold marginal pairs at anything but a great price; continue with strong hands and draws that are priced in.
A scare turn that helps their high-card range — an ace, a king, a straight-completer — makes the fold even clearer.
